Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Depressive symptom scores (CES-D) did not differ between T2DM patients with vitamin D insufficiency and those with normal vitamin D.
Sentence: "There was no significant difference between groups with regard to the indices of blood lipid, liver function, and scores in CES-D and PSQI."
Measured as: CES-D score
Population: 132 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
Intervention: Vitamin D insufficiency (plasma 25(OH)D <29 ng/mL), measured not given
Comparator: Normal vitamin D (25(OH)D ≥29 ng/mL)
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 132
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Vitamin D3 supplementation reduced depression scores more than placebo at 38-40 weeks of gestation.
Sentence: "While, the vitamin D group had greater reduction in depression scores than the control group at 38-40 weeks of gestation (p = 0.01) also, at 4 and 8 weeks after birth (p < 0.001)."
Measured as: depression score (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression scale) at 38-40 weeks of gestation
Population: Pregnant women in Shiraz, Iran, 18 or older, gestational age 26-28 weeks, baseline depression score 0-13, no history of mental illness
Intervention: Vitamin D3 2000 IU daily from 26-28 weeks of gestation until childbirth
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 169
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Study A is a cross-sectional comparison of vitamin D levels in diabetics, while Study B is a placebo-controlled RCT of supplementation in pregnant women, so the populations, exposures and designs all differ.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["intervention","comparator","design_or_bias"],"detail":"population: T2DM patients vs pregnant women 26-28 weeks; design: cross-sectional vs RCT with supplementation vs measured status"}
